title: Restricted Lie differentiation of affine group coactions
statement: Let $F$ be a field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field], and let $H$ be an affine group scheme of finite type over $F$ [def-sc-group-scheme]. Write $C=F[H]$ for its coordinate algebra, $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_F C$ for the map induced by multiplication, and $\varepsilon:C\to F$ for evaluation at the identity. A tangent vector at the identity is an $F$-linear map $x:C\to F$ satisfying $x(ab)=\varepsilon(a)x(b)+x(a)\varepsilon(b)$; these maps form $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(H)$. For such $x$ put $D_x=(\operatorname{id}_C\otimes x)\Delta:C\to C$. Then $x\mapsto D_x$ identifies $\mathfrak h$ with the left-invariant $F$-derivations of $C$, where a derivation $D$ is left-invariant if $\Delta D=(\operatorname{id}_C\otimes D)\Delta$. The commutator $[D_x,D_y]$ and the $p$th composition $D_x^p$ are left-invariant derivations. The operations defined by $D_{[x,y]}=[D_x,D_y]$ and $D_{x^{[p]}}=D_x^p$ make $\mathfrak h$ a restricted Lie algebra whose bracket agrees with the tangent bracket induced by group commutators, with the three restricted identities and the polynomials $s_i$ specified in [lem-sfb-restricted-pbw-basis]. If $f:H\to K$ is a homomorphism of affine finite-type $F$-group schemes and $f^*:F[K]\to C$ its coordinate map, its differential $df(x)=x\circ f^*$ preserves brackets and restricted operations. In particular every group automorphism of $H$ induces a restricted Lie automorphism of $\mathfrak h$. For any $F$-vector space $W$ with a counital coassociative coaction $\alpha:W\to W\otimes_F C$, the operators $\rho(x)=(\operatorname{id}_W\otimes x)\alpha$ satisfy $\rho([x,y])=\rho(x)\rho(y)-\rho(y)\rho(x)$ and $\rho(x^{[p]})=\rho(x)^p$. Consequently they define a unital action of $u(\mathfrak h)=T_F(\mathfrak h)/(xy-yx-[x,y],x^p-x^{[p]})$ on $W$, with no finite-dimensionality hypothesis on $W$.

source.place: Sections 10d and 10k, Theorem 10.23 and Proposition 10.38, printed pp.193--194 and 205--206; Theorem 11.25 and Proposition 11.26, printed pp.217--218, for invariant derivations; paragraph preceding Proposition 11.36, printed p.223, for the restricted operation; Section 10l, printed pp.207--208, for the distribution action on representations. The coaction formulas state explicitly its extension to arbitrary rational modules.

proof.text: Pulling back the associativity and identity diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme] gives coassociativity and both counit identities for $\Delta,\varepsilon$; both are algebra maps. Write $\Delta(a)=\sum a_1\otimes a_2$, with all tensor sums finite. The tangent Leibniz rule gives $D_x(ab)=\sum a_1b_1(\varepsilon(a_2)x(b_2)+x(a_2)\varepsilon(b_2))=aD_x(b)+D_x(a)b$. Coassociativity gives $\Delta D_x=(\operatorname{id}\otimes D_x)\Delta$, and the counit gives $\varepsilon D_x=x$. Conversely, for an invariant derivation $D$, $x=\varepsilon D$ is a tangent derivation and $D_x=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon D)\Delta=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta D=D$. These formulas prove the asserted linear bijection.

source.place: §11e, Theorem 11.25 and Proposition 11.26, pp.217–218; invariant specialization written out

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-convolution-linear-map-algebra] with $R=B=F$: the space $E=\operatorname{Hom}_F(C,F)$ has associative convolution $(\phi*\psi)(a)=\sum\phi(a_1)\psi(a_2)$ with unit $\varepsilon$. For every $\phi\in E$, set $R_\phi=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\phi)\Delta$. Coassociativity gives $R_\phi R_\psi(a)=\sum a_1\phi(a_2)\psi(a_3)=R_{\phi*\psi}(a)$, while $R_\varepsilon=\operatorname{id}$ and $\varepsilon R_\phi=\phi$. Thus $R:E\to\operatorname{End}_F(C)$ is an injective unital algebra map. In particular $R_x=D_x$.

source.place: §10l, p.208, convolution product; explicit regular-coaction calculation

proof.text: If $D,E$ are derivations, expansion of $DE(ab)-ED(ab)$ cancels the two mixed terms and yields $[D,E](ab)=[D,E](a)b+a[D,E](b)$. To handle $p$th composition, let $M_a$ denote multiplication by $a$ in $\operatorname{End}_F(C)$. The Leibniz rule says $[D,M_a]=M_{D(a)}$, hence $\operatorname{ad}(D)^p(M_a)=M_{D^p(a)}$. The first identity of [lem-sfb-associative-jacobson-identities], applied in the associative algebra $\operatorname{End}_F(C)$, identifies this with $[D^p,M_a]$. Evaluating at $b$ gives $D^p(ab)=D^p(a)b+aD^p(b)$. Finally if $D,E$ are invariant then $\Delta DE=(\operatorname{id}\otimes DE)\Delta$; subtraction and repeated composition show that $[D,E]$ and $D^p$ are invariant.

source.place: Proposition 10.38(a), pp.205–206; paragraph preceding Proposition 11.36, p.223; multiplication-operator argument for closure

proof.text: Use the inverse from step 1 to define $[x,y]$ and $x^{[p]}$ by $D_{[x,y]}=[D_x,D_y]$ and $D_{x^{[p]}}=D_x^p$. The commutator Lie algebra and its bracket-closed subspaces are those of [def-wf-lie-algebra], so this gives a Lie algebra. Apply [lem-sfb-associative-jacobson-identities] to $\operatorname{End}_F(C)$ and restrict to its invariant derivations: it gives $\operatorname{ad}(x^{[p]})=\operatorname{ad}(x)^p$ and the stated sum formula, since the linear bracket-preserving injection $x\mapsto D_x$ preserves each coefficient defining $s_i$. Also $(cD_x)^p=c^pD_x^p$ proves scalar semilinearity. Injectivity reflects all three identities. Step 2 additionally gives, inside $E$, $[x,y]=x*y-y*x$ and $x^{[p]}=x^{*p}$.

source.place: Proposition 10.38 and Definition 10.39, pp.205–207; restricted operation preceding Proposition 11.36, p.223

proof.text: Check the tangent bracket directly. Let $B=F[t,s]/(t^2,s^2)$. The tangent product rule and $x(1)=y(1)=0$ imply that $U=\varepsilon+tx$ and $V=\varepsilon+sy$ are algebra maps $C\to B$, hence $B$-points of $H$. Point multiplication is convolution, by the definition of $\Delta$. In the convolution algebra of [lem-sfb-convolution-linear-map-algebra], their inverses are $\varepsilon-tx$ and $\varepsilon-sy$. Expanding four factors, using $t^2=s^2=0$, gives $UVU^{-1}V^{-1}=\varepsilon+ts(x*y-y*x)$. Thus the mixed tangent coefficient of the group commutator is exactly the bracket from step 4, with the stated sign; this also covers $p=2$.

source.place: §10d, equations (60)–(63), Theorem 10.23, pp.192–194; explicit two-parameter commutator expansion

proof.text: For a group homomorphism $f:H\to K$, put $C_K=F[K]$. Pullback of multiplication and identity gives $\Delta_H f^*=(f^*\otimes f^*)\Delta_K$ and $\varepsilon_H f^*=\varepsilon_K$. The product rule then shows $x f^*$ is tangent. For arbitrary functionals, $(\phi*\psi)f^*=(\phi f^*)*(\psi f^*)$ by these displayed coalgebra identities. Therefore precomposition with $f^*$ preserves the convolution commutator and the $p$th convolution power, which are the tangent operations by step 4. This proves the two assertions about $df$. For a group automorphism, applying the same construction to its inverse gives the inverse differential, so it is a restricted Lie automorphism.

For the given $W,\alpha$, define $S_\phi=(\operatorname{id}_W\otimes\phi)\alpha$ for every $\phi\in E$. Coassociativity of $\alpha$ gives $S_\phi S_\psi(w)=\sum w_0\phi(c_1)\psi(c_2)=S_{\phi*\psi}(w)$, where $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\alpha(w)=\sum w_0\otimes c_1\otimes c_2$; counitality gives $S_\varepsilon=\operatorname{id}_W$. Thus $S$ is a unital algebra map and step 4 gives both required formulas for $\rho(x)=S_x$. Explicitly send a tensor word $x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n$ to $\rho(x_1)\cdots\rho(x_n)$, and the empty word to $\operatorname{id}_W$, extending linearly on the direct sum. This is well defined by multilinearity and multiplicative by concatenation. Each displayed generator of the defining ideal of $u(\mathfrak h)$ maps to zero by the two formulas, so the map factors through the quotient and defines its unital action. Every tensor expression used is a finite sum, regardless of $\dim_F W$.
